facts.label: Credit analysis by dimension
facts.text: Balance-sheet leverage rose in 2025 because earnings fell faster than debt, and it has been flat since. Carrying-value debt fell from USD 12,142 million at the end of 2024 to USD 11,784 million a year later, but reported EBITDA fell from USD 3,628 million to USD 3,275 million, so debt over EBITDA rose from 3.35x to 3.60x and net debt over EBITDA from 3.11x to 3.33x. Reported EBITDA for 2024 includes a net credit of USD 331 million in transaction and other costs, which the issuer attributes in part to gains on the sale of the WSOP trademark and the LINQ Promenade, so the issuer-adjusted measure, which fell from USD 3,739 million to USD 3,624 million, is the better guide to underlying earnings. A reduction of USD 584 million in carrying-value debt since the end of 2024 has been offset by last-twelve-months EBITDA falling further to USD 3,213 million, leaving net leverage at 3.33x. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 99–100; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; calculation C42; calculation C48; calculation C127

facts.label: Credit analysis by dimension
facts.text: The debt line understates the fixed claims on the business. Long-term financing obligations to VICI and GLPI of USD 13,188 million sit on their own balance sheet line and are not in Total Debt, yet their payments are treated as interest, so reported EBITDA is struck before about USD 1,370 million of rent over the last twelve months. Adding the obligations to debt gives 7.70x, against 3.60x on the balance-sheet definition, which is the better measure of the fixed claims that EBITDA has to meet. Secured principal of USD 9,320 million is 2.90x last-twelve-months EBITDA and ranks ahead of USD 2,300 million of senior unsecured notes. facts.text: Cash interest cover has been flat at about 1.52x because falling debt interest has been matched by falling EBITDA while rent interest rises. Cash interest on debt alone fell to USD 741 million over the last twelve months from USD 1,052 million in 2024 as debt was repaid and floating rates fell, but cash interest on the lease-style obligations kept rising to USD 1,370 million. facts.text: Cash-flow quality is acceptable but leans on lower capital spending. facts.label: Credit analysis by dimension
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a cautious view is that debt interest and debt are falling together. Carrying-value debt is down USD 584 million since the end of 2024, cash interest on debt has fallen by nearly 30%, the covenant tests the issuer reports for the CEI Revolving Credit Facility and Term Loan A (net total leverage 6.50:1 and fixed charge coverage 2.0:1) are stated as met at September 30, 2026, and cash interest for debt alone is covered 4.34x. That view would win if the landlords' escalators stayed near the current pace while EBITDA grew; it loses if the nine-month fall in issuer-adjusted EBITDA continues, because the rent leg does not fall with earnings. Covenant headroom is not calculated here because the covenant definitions are not supplied. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 52–53; calculation C127; calculation C80

limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- The issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is calculated as operating income plus depreciation and amortization for every income statement column; it includes impairment charges, transaction costs and stock-based compensation, and it differs from the issuer's Adjusted EBITDA by USD 349 million for 2025, which restricts comparison with the issuer's own leverage language and is a medium-severity gap closed by stating the basis beside every ratio. - Long-term financing obligations of USD 13,188 million to VICI and GLPI are outside Total Debt, and debt over EBITDA is 3.60x without them and 7.70x with them, so any leverage quote that omits the basis misstates the claim on EBITDA; this is a high-severity definition gap closed by always showing both rows. - Debt appears at principal, at the debt note's book value and at balance-sheet carrying value, and the issuer's net debt is on principal, so the same debt can be quoted at three figures; the differences tie to printed discounts and deferred finance charges and are logged as a medium-severity definition conflict, closed by using carrying value for ratios and naming the basis. - The quarterly reports carry no leases note, so lease and financing obligation maturities are known only at December 31, 2025 and the later balance sheet lines and cash interest are the only evidence for 2026; this limits any forecast of rent and is a medium-severity gap closed only by a later annual report. - The fourth quarter of 2025 is not reported alone, so revenue, reported EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA for that quarter are the full year less nine months and carry the full-year impairment of USD 182 million; this is a low-severity gap closed by the fourth-quarter release. - Cash interest paid for other financing obligations is printed only from the second quarter of 2026 and for some 2025 comparatives, so it is kept outside cash interest paid for comparability; the amount is USD 7 million for the nine months of 2026, which makes this a low-severity gap. - The filings print dashes or no line for several items in particular periods, including the loss on extinguishment of debt in the 2026 columns, income taxes in the first half of 2026, impairment charges and asset acquisition payments in the interim cash flows, and these are recorded as not supplied rather than zero; the printed totals foot without them, so the effect on every total is nil and the gap is low severity. - Interim cash flow statements are year to date, so discrete second-quarter and third-quarter cash flows are not shown; they would be derived and are not needed for the last-twelve-months construction, which makes this a low-severity gap. - Borrowing capacity at December 31, 2024 is not printed in the 2025 annual report, so the liquidity chart states undrawn facilities as not supplied for that date; the gap is low severity and is closed by the 2024 annual report. - The margin, floor and amortization of the Caesars Virginia facilities are not stated, so those terms are gaps in the debt instrument table; this is a low-severity gap. Separately, the debt table lists the Special Improvement District Bonds and the long-term notes and other payables, USD 39 million of principal in total, as unsecured debt but states no rank, so they are left out of the debt stack; this is also a low-severity gap. - The segment perimeter changed on March 3, 2026 when Caesars Windsor moved from Managed and Branded to Regional, and the issuer states that later periods are not fully comparable with earlier ones, which limits like-for-like segment trends and is a low-severity gap. - How the pending merger is financed and what happens to the existing notes and loans at closing are not described in any supplied document, so pro forma net debt and leverage are not established and the post-balance-sheet table records no event; this is a high-severity gap closed by the merger agreement and the merger proxy statement. - The sources carry no balance sheet at September 30, 2025, so debt, cash and net debt for the nine months of 2025 are not supplied in the financials table, and nine-month leverage and cover are not calculable because a nine-month period is not a twelve-month EBITDA base; this is a low-severity gap that does not affect the fiscal-year or last-twelve-months ratios. - The 2024 Adjusted EBITDA is USD 3,739 million in the segment table and USD 3,723 million after a pre-disposition adjustment of USD 16 million in the reconciliation; the larger figure is used and the gap is low severity.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: The pending transaction is a cash merger in which Fertitta Gaming Holdco, LLC, through Empire Merger Sub, Inc., acquires Caesars Entertainment, Inc. for USD 31.00 per share, plus a daily per-share ticking fee if closing has not occurred by June 26, 2027. The agreement was signed on May 27, 2026, the board recommended it, stockholders approved it on September 22, 2026, and closing is subject to expiry of the antitrust waiting period and certain gaming approvals. Either side may terminate if closing has not occurred by May 27, 2027, an end date that extends automatically to August 27, 2027 and then November 27, 2027 when only those approvals are outstanding. The company owes a termination fee of USD 200 million in defined circumstances and the buyer owes a reverse termination fee of USD 450 million if regulatory approvals fail or the end date passes with only those approvals outstanding. facts.label: Ownership and group structure
facts.text: Caesars is a listed company with a single class of common stock, no identified controlling holder, a founding family and an investor agreement whose terms are not supplied, and a pending sale to Fertitta Gaming Holdco, LLC. The parent borrows for the group and its material wholly owned domestic subsidiaries guarantee the secured and unsecured debt, with 79.94% of principal secured by substantially all assets. The Caesars Virginia facilities of USD 371 million, 3.18% of principal, are secured only by that venture's assets and are not guaranteed by the parent, and the venture's partner received USD 65 million of distributions in nine months 2026. Leased casinos and the lease obligations sit alongside the debt, and a lease termination could cross into the debt agreements. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is volume-and-hold driven rather than contracted. Group net revenues rose 2.7% in nine months 2026 on casino growth, but Las Vegas fell 2.0% as fewer city-wide conventions and weaker leisure visitation cut occupancy and rates, while Regional rose 6.1% with Caesars Windsor consolidated and Caesars Digital rose 6.3% on iGaming handle and hold. Hold is volatile and sits inside typical ranges the company states, so reported growth can reverse without a change in demand, and Las Vegas hotel rates compressed instead of rising. For creditors this means revenue is predictable only within a band and the Las Vegas component has the least visibility. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 41–47; calculation D16

facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Costs are heavy in labor, gaming taxes and fixed rent, which makes margins hard to defend. Gaming taxes were 15.73% of net revenues against 15.03% a year earlier, about 21,000 of about 50,000 team members are covered by collective bargaining agreements, and corporate costs rose 24.8%. Las Vegas lost USD 102 million of Adjusted EBITDA on USD 59 million less revenue, and Regional kept 23.13% of added revenue against a 31.3% margin, so operating leverage is working against the group. Marketing and capital expenditure are the main discretionary levers, while rent is fixed. facts.text: Free cash flow after capital expenditure converts only 16.29% of last-twelve-months issuer-adjusted EBITDA, because cash interest on debt and rent absorb 59.08% of it and capital expenditure of USD 664 million takes much of the rest. Capital expenditure of USD 507 million in nine months 2026 was below USD 648 million a year earlier, and the 2026 plan of USD 667 million to USD 712 million includes USD 357 million to USD 377 million of maintenance. Seasonality in Regional markets and event timing in Las Vegas shift quarterly cash, and customer deposits and other deferred revenue fell to USD 449 million from USD 492 million, a small drag. EBITDA therefore turns into debt-service cash thinly and unevenly. facts.label: Competitive forces
facts.text: Rivalry is intense: the company describes new casinos, tribal expansion and large Las Vegas developments, and it took 2025 impairments in three Regional reporting units because localized competition lowered expected cash flows, so rivalry already reduces asset values. New entrants face licensing barriers, but new online jurisdictions and tribal supply still add competition. Substitutes are growing: prediction markets, sweepstakes products, daily fantasy sports and lotteries compete for the same spend. Buyer power is high because customers can switch properties and apps, and promotional spending in digital was USD 249 million in nine months. Supplier power sits with unions, performers and the landlords who set rent; the landlords are the most material for creditors. facts.text: Regulation and taxes are material to credit because gaming taxes take 15.73% of revenue and are raised on digital wagers in some states, and because the merger needs gaming approvals. These factors change leverage, free cash flow and refinancing capacity, so they are primary drivers rather than background. facts.text: Strengths: liquidity of USD 2,947 million with USD 142 million due before 2028, falling debt and debt interest, four diversified segments, and flexibility in growth capital expenditure. Weaknesses: lease-style obligations outside debt, falling Las Vegas earnings, 47.48% of principal due in 2029 and 2030, and thin goodwill cushions. Opportunities that could improve credit: iGaming growth in new states, payback from recent Regional capital expenditure at Lake Tahoe and New Orleans, and a merger that leaves debt in place or repays it from equity. Threats that could weaken credit: a leveraged buyout structure, persistent Las Vegas softness, higher gaming taxes and substitution by prediction markets. facts.text: The financial profile rests on adequate liquidity and falling debt, and is constrained by fixed charges and a weak cash conversion. facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over the next 12 to 24 months the credit depends on Las Vegas stabilising, the merger path and the 2028 maturities. Management expects strong free cash flow in 2026 on operating momentum, lower cash interest and lower capital expenditure, and the 2026 results to date are consistent with that, but Las Vegas, Regional margins and the lease escalator in November 2026 are headwinds. The merger's outside date can extend to November 27, 2027, and the revolver and Term Loan A mature on January 31, 2028, so refinancing must be addressed inside that window. Over three to five years the rent schedule rises to USD 1,468 million in 2030 while USD 5,536 million of debt matures in 2029 and 2030; digital legalization and capital expenditure payback are tailwinds, and gaming taxes, labor and competition are headwinds. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The downside starts with Las Vegas visitation and convention demand staying weak while Regional margins keep compressing under labor and gaming-tax costs. The first break is Adjusted EBITDA falling faster than revenue, as Las Vegas already did, and rent and debt interest do not fall with it. A 16.29% fall in issuer-adjusted EBITDA would erase free cash flow and would take lease-adjusted debt to 8.27x from 6.93x, and cutting growth and digital capital expenditure would extend that point to a 24.97% to 25.66% fall. Liquidity of USD 2,947 million and no material maturity before 2028 mean resilience looks sufficient to avoid distress for roughly a year, but the revolver and Term Loan A would then need extending from weaker earnings. The scenario is an illustration at the break-even point, not a forecast, and the observable triggers are Las Vegas Adjusted EBITDA, Regional margin, revolver drawings and any extension of the 2028 facilities. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Caesars presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, segment diversification, a loyalty program and an owned digital platform, but credit quality is constrained by USD 13,188 million of lease-style obligations outside debt, falling Las Vegas earnings and thin cash conversion. Cash-flow durability appears adequate for the next year and weak against a sustained earnings decline. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on extending the revolver and Term Loan A before January 2028, on the treatment of existing debt in the merger and on stable earnings into the 2029 and 2030 maturities. The primary downside path is Las Vegas and Regional earnings declining against fixed and escalating rent. Further analysis would require the merger financing terms, the executed debt and lease documents, covenant definitions and peer data. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: earnings decline against fixed lease-style obligations. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0); calculation D5; calculation D14

## Findings
### Bottom line

The seven supplied Caesars Entertainment documents support a credit snapshot of the consolidated company, but creditor conclusions on covenants, ratings, valuation and the pending merger's effect on existing debt cannot be drawn from them.

The annual report and the three quarterly reports give audited and unaudited statements, facility-level debt, liquidity and segment data to September 30, 2026, so Financial foundation, Business & governance and Fundamental credit can proceed with stated limitations. The fourth quarter of 2025 is not reported on its own, and the merger with Fertitta Gaming is described only in the company's own reports: how the buyer finances it and what happens to existing notes and loans at closing are not established. Ratings, peers, market prices and executed legal documents were not supplied, so the modules that need them cannot be assessed from these sources.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Caesars is more leveraged than its balance-sheet debt suggests: debt is 3.60x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA, but adding the VICI and GLPI financing obligations lifts that to 7.70x, and EBITDA covers all cash interest, including that rent, only 1.52x.

Near-term liquidity is adequate, with cash of USD 864 million and net revolver availability of USD 2,083 million, and only USD 142 million of principal falls due before 2028, but USD 5,536 million matures in 2029 and 2030. Free cash flow after capital expenditure was USD 582 million over the last twelve months against USD 11,558 million of debt, and how the pending merger affects that debt is not established.

### Credit analysis by dimension

Balance-sheet leverage rose in 2025 because earnings fell faster than debt, and it has been flat since. Carrying-value debt fell from USD 12,142 million at the end of 2024 to USD 11,784 million a year later, but reported EBITDA fell from USD 3,628 million to USD 3,275 million, so debt over EBITDA rose from 3.35x to 3.60x and net debt over EBITDA from 3.11x to 3.33x. Reported EBITDA for 2024 includes a net credit of USD 331 million in transaction and other costs, which the issuer attributes in part to gains on the sale of the WSOP trademark and the LINQ Promenade, so the issuer-adjusted measure, which fell from USD 3,739 million to USD 3,624 million, is the better guide to underlying earnings. A reduction of USD 584 million in carrying-value debt since the end of 2024 has been offset by last-twelve-months EBITDA falling further to USD 3,213 million, leaving net leverage at 3.33x.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 99–100; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; calculation C42; calculation C48; calculation C127

The debt line understates the fixed claims on the business. Long-term financing obligations to VICI and GLPI of USD 13,188 million sit on their own balance sheet line and are not in Total Debt, yet their payments are treated as interest, so reported EBITDA is struck before about USD 1,370 million of rent over the last twelve months. Adding the obligations to debt gives 7.70x, against 3.60x on the balance-sheet definition, which is the better measure of the fixed claims that EBITDA has to meet. Secured principal of USD 9,320 million is 2.90x last-twelve-months EBITDA and ranks ahead of USD 2,300 million of senior unsecured notes.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 5, 15–16; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 117–118; calculation C79; calculation C129; calculation C124; calculation C125; calculation C126

Cash interest cover has been flat at about 1.52x because falling debt interest has been matched by falling EBITDA while rent interest rises. Cash interest on debt alone fell to USD 741 million over the last twelve months from USD 1,052 million in 2024 as debt was repaid and floating rates fell, but cash interest on the lease-style obligations kept rising to USD 1,370 million. All cash interest absorbs 65.70% of last-twelve-months EBITDA, which leaves little room for a decline in earnings before free cash flow turns negative. On cash interest for debt alone, cover would be 4.34x, which is the right figure only if the landlords can be ignored.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 101; calculation C67; calculation C80; calculation C128

Cash-flow quality is acceptable but leans on lower capital spending. Operating cash flow was USD 942 million for the first nine months of 2026 against USD 998 million a year earlier, while purchases of property and equipment fell by USD 141 million, which lifted free cash flow after capital expenditure to USD 435 million from USD 350 million. Issuer-adjusted EBITDA for the nine months fell by USD 51 million, so the whole improvement in free cash flow comes from lower capital spending, not from earnings or operating cash flow, and the last-twelve-months free cash flow of USD 582 million is 5.04% of debt. Distributions to noncontrolling owners of USD 65 million and financing obligation payments of USD 29 million are further uses after that free cash flow.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; calculation C133; calculation C134; calculation C102; calculation C103; calculation C131

Liquidity is adequate for the next year and a half, but the maturity profile concentrates after that. Cash of USD 864 million plus net revolver availability of USD 2,083 million gives USD 2,947 million, against only USD 142 million of principal due from October 2026 to the end of 2027. The CEI Revolving Credit Facility and Term Loan A mature on January 31, 2028, which leaves the revolver, the source of that availability, with less than twelve months to run from the end of January 2027, and USD 5,536 million, or 47.48% of principal, matures in 2029 and 2030. The Caesars Virginia revolver of USD 25 million is counted in the issuer's liquidity but serves that joint venture only.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-10-27_ex991-2026q3ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 15–19; calculation C88; calculation C94; calculation C95; calculation C96

Non-debt funding float is small and shrinking. Customer deposits and other deferred revenue were USD 449 million at the end of September 2026, down USD 100 million from USD 549 million at the end of 2024; the annual report attributes the 2025 decline mainly to lower gaming deposits and states no cause for the 2026 decline, which is a modest drag on operating cash flow, not a funding stress, and the outstanding chip liability and Caesars Rewards obligations are each below USD 100 million.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 132–133; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 22; calculation C130

The strongest evidence against a cautious view is that debt interest and debt are falling together. Carrying-value debt is down USD 584 million since the end of 2024, cash interest on debt has fallen by nearly 30%, the covenant tests the issuer reports for the CEI Revolving Credit Facility and Term Loan A (net total leverage 6.50:1 and fixed charge coverage 2.0:1) are stated as met at September 30, 2026, and cash interest for debt alone is covered 4.34x. That view would win if the landlords' escalators stayed near the current pace while EBITDA grew; it loses if the nine-month fall in issuer-adjusted EBITDA continues, because the rent leg does not fall with earnings. Covenant headroom is not calculated here because the covenant definitions are not supplied.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 52–53; calculation C127; calculation C80

Subsequent events are flagged and kept out of period figures. The merger agreement of May 27, 2026 and the stockholder approval of September 22, 2026 describe a cash merger at USD 31.00 a share that has not closed; the filings state no financing for it and no treatment of the existing notes and loans, so pro forma net debt and leverage are not established and the post-balance-sheet table records no event. The acquisitions of Caesars Windsor on March 3, 2026 and the remaining interest in Grand Bazaar on May 1, 2026 are inside the 2026 columns, with USD 98 million of asset acquisition payments in the cash flow, and the segment perimeter changed on the first date.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–10; EX-99.1_2026-04-28_ex991-2026q1ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 2

Data-quality and definition risks are limited and logged. Every statement foots to its printed totals, the cash flow ties to the balance sheet cash and restricted cash, and each fiscal-year ratio ties to its statement lines. Four definitions need care when figures are quoted: debt on principal against carrying value, the issuer's net debt against net debt on carrying value, reported against issuer-adjusted EBITDA (a difference of USD 349 million for 2025), and the lease-style obligations outside debt. The fourth quarter of 2025 is not reported alone and is shown as the full year less nine months. Dashes in the filings are recorded as not supplied rather than zero.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 99–102; calculation C132; calculation C92; calculation C93

## Gaps

- The issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is calculated as operating income plus depreciation and amortization for every income statement column; it includes impairment charges, transaction costs and stock-based compensation, and it differs from the issuer's Adjusted EBITDA by USD 349 million for 2025, which restricts comparison with the issuer's own leverage language and is a medium-severity gap closed by stating the basis beside every ratio.

- Long-term financing obligations of USD 13,188 million to VICI and GLPI are outside Total Debt, and debt over EBITDA is 3.60x without them and 7.70x with them, so any leverage quote that omits the basis misstates the claim on EBITDA; this is a high-severity definition gap closed by always showing both rows.

- Debt appears at principal, at the debt note's book value and at balance-sheet carrying value, and the issuer's net debt is on principal, so the same debt can be quoted at three figures; the differences tie to printed discounts and deferred finance charges and are logged as a medium-severity definition conflict, closed by using carrying value for ratios and naming the basis.

- The quarterly reports carry no leases note, so lease and financing obligation maturities are known only at December 31, 2025 and the later balance sheet lines and cash interest are the only evidence for 2026; this limits any forecast of rent and is a medium-severity gap closed only by a later annual report.

- The fourth quarter of 2025 is not reported alone, so revenue, reported EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA for that quarter are the full year less nine months and carry the full-year impairment of USD 182 million; this is a low-severity gap closed by the fourth-quarter release.

- Cash interest paid for other financing obligations is printed only from the second quarter of 2026 and for some 2025 comparatives, so it is kept outside cash interest paid for comparability; the amount is USD 7 million for the nine months of 2026, which makes this a low-severity gap.

- The filings print dashes or no line for several items in particular periods, including the loss on extinguishment of debt in the 2026 columns, income taxes in the first half of 2026, impairment charges and asset acquisition payments in the interim cash flows, and these are recorded as not supplied rather than zero; the printed totals foot without them, so the effect on every total is nil and the gap is low severity.

- Interim cash flow statements are year to date, so discrete second-quarter and third-quarter cash flows are not shown; they would be derived and are not needed for the last-twelve-months construction, which makes this a low-severity gap.

- Borrowing capacity at December 31, 2024 is not printed in the 2025 annual report, so the liquidity chart states undrawn facilities as not supplied for that date; the gap is low severity and is closed by the 2024 annual report.

- The margin, floor and amortization of the Caesars Virginia facilities are not stated, so those terms are gaps in the debt instrument table; this is a low-severity gap. Separately, the debt table lists the Special Improvement District Bonds and the long-term notes and other payables, USD 39 million of principal in total, as unsecured debt but states no rank, so they are left out of the debt stack; this is also a low-severity gap.

- The segment perimeter changed on March 3, 2026 when Caesars Windsor moved from Managed and Branded to Regional, and the issuer states that later periods are not fully comparable with earlier ones, which limits like-for-like segment trends and is a low-severity gap.

- How the pending merger is financed and what happens to the existing notes and loans at closing are not described in any supplied document, so pro forma net debt and leverage are not established and the post-balance-sheet table records no event; this is a high-severity gap closed by the merger agreement and the merger proxy statement.

- The sources carry no balance sheet at September 30, 2025, so debt, cash and net debt for the nine months of 2025 are not supplied in the financials table, and nine-month leverage and cover are not calculable because a nine-month period is not a twelve-month EBITDA base; this is a low-severity gap that does not affect the fiscal-year or last-twelve-months ratios.

- The 2024 Adjusted EBITDA is USD 3,739 million in the segment table and USD 3,723 million after a pre-disposition adjustment of USD 16 million in the reconciliation; the larger figure is used and the gap is low severity.

spans.text: # Business & governance for Caesars Entertainment, Inc. (czr), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Business and governance assessment for Caesars Entertainment, Inc. (issuer czr) as of 2026-11-05 on the credit_snapshot pathway. The scope is the business and operating model, ownership and control, the pending merger, and governance and sponsor behaviour, from the seven supplied SEC documents.
## Sources

| EX-99.1_2026-07-28_ex991-2026q2ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl | Earnings release (Exhibit 99.1) for the second quarter of 2026 | 2026-07-28 (release date) | 89cd5ad8c7a0d45cdf4a8f6462fc3964a9e7d04aae46811b1f50bebeb80c1762 | Second-quarter segment trend |

| CP-0 | Source readiness (CP-0), the supplied source-readiness handoff for this run | 41a439bc8a5d2710703ed2fbb53d7212650697e2be4bec0b83c2d4805ebb7638 |
## Findings
### Bottom line

Caesars is a diversified but rent-burdened casino operator whose creditors face an ownership change, and the supplied documents do not establish how the buyer finances it or what happens to existing debt.

Adjusted EBITDA for nine months 2026 was USD 2,672 million, down from USD 2,723 million, as Regional growth of 4.5% only partly offset Las Vegas at minus 8.0%. Cash interest paid on the VICI and GLPI leases took 38.55% of that Adjusted EBITDA and cash interest on debt a further 21.71%. Fertitta Gaming agreed on May 27, 2026 to buy the company for USD 31.00 per share in cash, stockholders approved on September 22, 2026, and regulatory approvals remain. Management itself lists increased leverage from the transaction as a risk.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 31–32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 45–46; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 57; EX-99.1_2026-10-27_ex991-2026q3ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation B10; calculation B17
### Key findings

- Earnings are diversified by segment but concentrated in two of them. Regional and Las Vegas produced 49.37% and 47.68% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA, Caesars Digital 6.51% and Managed and Branded 1.85%, while corporate costs took 5.41%.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 68; calculation B2

- Las Vegas is the segment under pressure and carries 44.12% of nine-month Adjusted EBITDA. Its Adjusted EBITDA fell 8.0% in the first nine months of 2026, to USD 1,179 million from USD 1,281 million, and its margin fell to 40.0% from 42.6%, on fewer city-wide conventions, lower leisure visitation and softer hotel occupancy and rates.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 45–46; calculation B4

- Regional and digital growth is real but partly reflects perimeter change and hold. Regional Adjusted EBITDA rose 4.5% to USD 1,447 million, helped by consolidating Caesars Windsor from March 3, 2026. Caesars Digital rose 19.9% to USD 181 million, yet its quarterly Adjusted EBITDA swung from minus 15.0% in the second quarter to plus 57.1% in the third, which fits the company's own warning that hold and promotional spending move digital results. The Windsor contribution is not separated.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 46–47; EX-99.1_2026-07-28_ex991-2026q2ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 1; EX-99.1_2026-10-27_ex991-2026q3ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 1

- Rent to landlords is the largest fixed claim on cash flow and sits outside the debt table. Caesars leases 25 of its 47 casinos, 18 from VICI and six from GLPI, and cash interest paid on those leases was USD 1,030 million in nine months 2026 against USD 580 million of cash interest on debt. Financing obligations of USD 13,188 million exceed debt principal of USD 11,659 million, and a lease default could let a landlord terminate and trigger a default under the debt agreements.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 50; EX-99.1_2026-10-27_ex991-2026q3ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation B7; calculation B10

- Control is about to change and creditor treatment is unestablished. The cash price is about USD 6,318 million on the shares outstanding, closing needs antitrust waiting-period expiry and gaming approvals, and a USD 450 million reverse termination fee is payable by the buyer if regulatory approvals fail. How the buyer finances the purchase, who owns the buyer and what happens to existing notes and loans are not stated.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation B11; calculation B12

- Governance shows no extraction in the supplied documents, but founding-family influence and the rights under the Icahn agreement cannot be sized. Eleven directors signed the annual report, an executive chairman among them, and an agreement with Icahn entities covers director appointment, but its terms and every holder's stake are not supplied. No sponsor fees or dividends appear, and the one related-party lease costs USD 0.6 million a year. Sponsor and governance risk is Medium on current evidence.

- Capital allocation has turned toward debt reduction in 2026. No shares were repurchased in nine months 2026 against USD 179 million a year earlier, debt principal fell USD 246 million to USD 11,659 million and capital expenditure fell to USD 507 million from USD 648 million. Buybacks are not expected while the merger is pending, but a USD 221 million authorisation remains.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; EX-99.1_2026-10-27_ex991-2026q3ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation B14; calculation B15
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a cautious view is liquidity and a light near-term maturity profile. Cash was USD 864 million and cash plus revolver capacity totalled USD 2,947 million, no revolver was drawn, and only USD 28 million of principal falls due in the rest of 2026 and USD 114 million in 2027. The company reports compliance with its financial covenants, the leverage covenant being 6.50x, and the reverse termination fee gives the company a cash backstop if regulatory approvals fail.

The view would improve if the merger documents show existing notes and loans staying in place on unchanged terms or repaid from buyer equity, or if Las Vegas earnings stabilise. It would worsen if the transaction adds debt at the company or triggers repayment obligations on a change of control, or if the Las Vegas decline persists while rent escalates with consumer prices.
### Limitations

- Shareholdings of the Icahn entities, the founding family and other holders are not stated, so the conclusion that no holder is shown to control the company cannot be confirmed, and a large block would raise the weight placed on that holder's interests.

- The merger agreement, the merger proxy statement, the credit agreement and the indentures are not supplied, so the conclusions on post-closing leverage and on change-of-control treatment of notes, loans and leases rest on the company's summary and could move either way.

- Board independence, committee membership and compensation are incorporated by reference to a proxy statement that is not supplied, so the Medium sponsor and governance level covers only the facts visible in the annual and quarterly reports.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 156

- The quarterly reports carry no lease note, so the rent conclusion rests on the December 31, 2025 payment schedule plus cash interest paid and the remaining-2026 estimate, and later lease changes would alter it.

- Caesars Windsor is consolidated from March 3, 2026 and Grand Bazaar from May 1, 2026, and their contribution is not stated, so the Regional and Las Vegas trends overstate or understate like-for-like performance by an unstated amount.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The pending transaction is a cash merger in which Fertitta Gaming Holdco, LLC, through Empire Merger Sub, Inc., acquires Caesars Entertainment, Inc. for USD 31.00 per share, plus a daily per-share ticking fee if closing has not occurred by June 26, 2027. The agreement was signed on May 27, 2026, the board recommended it, stockholders approved it on September 22, 2026, and closing is subject to expiry of the antitrust waiting period and certain gaming approvals. Either side may terminate if closing has not occurred by May 27, 2027, an end date that extends automatically to August 27, 2027 and then November 27, 2027 when only those approvals are outstanding. The company owes a termination fee of USD 200 million in defined circumstances and the buyer owes a reverse termination fee of USD 450 million if regulatory approvals fail or the end date passes with only those approvals outstanding.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–9

The supplied documents do not describe how the buyer finances the price, who owns Fertitta Gaming Holdco, LLC, who holds the rollover shares, or whether existing notes, term loans and leases are repaid, assumed or left in place. Management lists the risk that required financing is not obtained on anticipated terms and the risk of increased leverage from the transaction. The company reported merger costs of USD 22 million for nine months 2026.

No new notes or term loans were issued in the first nine months of 2026: the debt table shows the same instruments as at year-end 2025 with the revolver repaid, and the most recent issue was USD 1.1 billion of senior notes due 2032 on October 17, 2024. In July 2025 the company redeemed all USD 546 million of its notes due 2027 using revolver borrowings and USD 225 million of proceeds from the WSOP note receivable, with a loss on extinguishment of about USD 4 million.

spans.text: # Fundamental credit for Caesars Entertainment, Inc. (czr), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Fundamental credit assessment for Caesars Entertainment, Inc. (issuer czr) as of 2026-11-05 on the credit_snapshot pathway. The scope is the business and financial profile, outlook, downside path and monitoring triggers, drawn from the seven supplied SEC documents and the three earlier module handoffs.
## Sources

## Findings
### Bottom line

Caesars has adequate liquidity and four operating segments, but USD 13,188 million of lease-style obligations outside debt, falling earnings and a change of control with undisclosed financing leave creditors exposed to an earnings decline more than to a near-term refinancing.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–9; calculation D5

Debt is 3.60x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA but 7.70x with those obligations, and EBITDA covers all cash interest, rent included, only 1.52x. Free cash flow of USD 582 million is 5.04% of debt, and a 16.29% fall in issuer-adjusted EBITDA would erase it. Liquidity of USD 2,947 million and only USD 142 million of principal due before 2028 give time, but 47.48% of principal matures in 2029 and 2030.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation D5; calculation D6; calculation D8; calculation D9; calculation D14
### Key findings

- Business risk is moderate: the group is diversified across four segments and many jurisdictions, but earnings sit in two of them. Las Vegas and Regional produced 97.05% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA, while Caesars Digital produced 6.51% and corporate costs took 5.41%, so a shock to either large segment reaches creditors directly.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 68; calculation D15

- Earnings are eroding slowly while revenue grows. Last-twelve-months issuer-adjusted EBITDA of USD 3,573 million is 4.44% below FY2024 and its margin fell to 30.49% from 33.25%; in nine months 2026 revenue rose USD 233 million but Adjusted EBITDA fell USD 51 million, because Las Vegas lost USD 102 million on USD 59 million less revenue and Regional kept only 23.13% of its added revenue.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 41–46; calculation D2; calculation D3; calculation D4; calculation D16

- Fixed claims outside debt dominate the credit. Lease-style obligations to VICI and GLPI of USD 13,188 million lift leverage to 7.70x from 3.60x, and all cash interest, rent included, absorbs 65.70% of last-twelve-months reported EBITDA. The contractual rent schedule rises to USD 1,468 million in 2030 from USD 1,369 million in 2026, so fixed charges grow while earnings fall, and a lease default could reach the debt agreements.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 50; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 117; calculation D5; calculation D7; calculation D12

- Cash generation is adequate but thin and leans on capital spending cuts. Free cash flow after capital expenditure was USD 582 million over the last twelve months, 5.04% of debt, and the nine-month improvement came from capital expenditure falling to USD 507 million from USD 648 million, not from earnings. Cutting every growth and digital project, USD 310 million to USD 335 million in 2026, would let issuer-adjusted EBITDA fall 24.97% to 25.66% before free cash flow turns negative, other things equal.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation D8; calculation D9; calculation D10; calculation D11

- Liquidity is adequate for the next year, and the refinancing test comes from 2028. Cash of USD 864 million and net revolver availability of USD 2,083 million total USD 2,947 million against only USD 142 million of principal due before 2028, but the revolver and Term Loan A mature on January 31, 2028 and USD 5,536 million, or 47.48% of principal, falls due in 2029 and 2030.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 16–18; calculation D14

- Rate exposure is unhedged. Floating-rate borrowings of USD 5,800 million, about half of debt, are carried with no derivatives, so each 100 bp rise adds about USD 58 million of interest, 9.97% of last-twelve-months free cash flow.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 54; calculation D13

- Financial policy was creditor-supportive in 2026 but control is changing. No shares were repurchased in nine months 2026, debt principal fell USD 246 million and no dividends are paid, yet the pending cash merger with Fertitta Gaming leaves the buyer's financing and the treatment of existing debt unstated, and management lists increased leverage as a risk. Sponsor and governance risk is Medium.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 57; EX-99.1_2026-10-27_ex991-2026q3ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 2
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against the cautious view is that debt and debt interest are both falling while liquidity covers the next year. Cash interest on debt fell to USD 741 million over the last twelve months from USD 1,052 million in FY2024, debt principal is USD 246 million lower since December 2025, cash interest on debt alone is covered 4.34x, the company reports compliance with its financial covenants, and a USD 450 million reverse termination fee is owed to the company if regulatory approvals fail. The view would improve if Las Vegas earnings stabilise while rent escalators stay near the scheduled 1.52% to 2.30% a year, or if the merger documents show existing debt staying in place or repaid from buyer equity.

It would worsen if Las Vegas keeps losing earnings faster than revenue, if Regional margins keep compressing, if the transaction adds debt at the company or triggers repayment on a change of control, or if the revolver and Term Loan A are not extended well before January 2028, when less than twelve months of life would remain from January 2027.

### Strengths and weaknesses

The main strengths are, first, liquidity and a light maturity profile: cash and net revolver availability of USD 2,947 million against USD 142 million of principal due before 2028 give creditors about a year of cover before refinancing matters. Second, debt reduction and falling interest on debt: principal is USD 246 million lower since December 2025 and cash interest on debt fell 29.56% from FY2024. Third, diversification with growth where it is wanted: Regional Adjusted EBITDA rose 4.5% and Caesars Digital 19.9% in nine months 2026, offsetting part of the Las Vegas decline. Fourth, capital expenditure flexibility: USD 310 million to USD 335 million of growth and digital spending in 2026 could be cut to protect cash.

The main weaknesses are, first, lease-style obligations of USD 13,188 million outside debt, which take total cash interest cover to 1.52x and rise on a contractual schedule. Second, falling earnings: issuer-adjusted EBITDA is 4.44% below FY2024 and Las Vegas fell 8.0% in nine months 2026. Third, maturity concentration: the revolver and Term Loan A mature on January 31, 2028 and USD 5,536 million falls due in 2029 and 2030. Fourth, a change of control whose financing and treatment of existing debt are not stated. Fifth, a thin valuation cushion: USD 2.5 billion of goodwill sits in five reporting units whose fair value did not significantly exceed carrying value.

### Company description

Caesars owns, leases, brands or manages 54 properties in 20 jurisdictions, runs retail and online sports betting in 35 jurisdictions and iGaming in six, and earns 57.61% of revenue from casino gaming, 16.93% from hotels and 14.92% from food and beverage. That mix is discretionary and cyclical, but it is spread across four segments, a loyalty program that links the properties and an owned digital platform, which supports cash-flow visibility better than a single-site operator. Of 47 casinos, 25 are leased, 24 of them from VICI and GLPI, so a large share of cash flow is committed to landlords before debt service, and gaming licences, tax rates and regulators set the operating terms.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 69; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; calculation D17
### Ownership and group structure

Caesars is a listed company with a single class of common stock, no identified controlling holder, a founding family and an investor agreement whose terms are not supplied, and a pending sale to Fertitta Gaming Holdco, LLC. The parent borrows for the group and its material wholly owned domestic subsidiaries guarantee the secured and unsecured debt, with 79.94% of principal secured by substantially all assets. The Caesars Virginia facilities of USD 371 million, 3.18% of principal, are secured only by that venture's assets and are not guaranteed by the parent, and the venture's partner received USD 65 million of distributions in nine months 2026. Leased casinos and the lease obligations sit alongside the debt, and a lease termination could cross into the debt agreements.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 15–16; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 50; calculation D16
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is volume-and-hold driven rather than contracted. Group net revenues rose 2.7% in nine months 2026 on casino growth, but Las Vegas fell 2.0% as fewer city-wide conventions and weaker leisure visitation cut occupancy and rates, while Regional rose 6.1% with Caesars Windsor consolidated and Caesars Digital rose 6.3% on iGaming handle and hold. Hold is volatile and sits inside typical ranges the company states, so reported growth can reverse without a change in demand, and Las Vegas hotel rates compressed instead of rising. For creditors this means revenue is predictable only within a band and the Las Vegas component has the least visibility.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 41–47; calculation D16
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Costs are heavy in labor, gaming taxes and fixed rent, which makes margins hard to defend. Gaming taxes were 15.73% of net revenues against 15.03% a year earlier, about 21,000 of about 50,000 team members are covered by collective bargaining agreements, and corporate costs rose 24.8%. Las Vegas lost USD 102 million of Adjusted EBITDA on USD 59 million less revenue, and Regional kept 23.13% of added revenue against a 31.3% margin, so operating leverage is working against the group. Marketing and capital expenditure are the main discretionary levers, while rent is fixed.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 45–48; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 16; calculation D16; calculation D18
### Capital intensity and cash flow conversion

Free cash flow after capital expenditure converts only 16.29% of last-twelve-months issuer-adjusted EBITDA, because cash interest on debt and rent absorb 59.08% of it and capital expenditure of USD 664 million takes much of the rest. Capital expenditure of USD 507 million in nine months 2026 was below USD 648 million a year earlier, and the 2026 plan of USD 667 million to USD 712 million includes USD 357 million to USD 377 million of maintenance. Seasonality in Regional markets and event timing in Las Vegas shift quarterly cash, and customer deposits and other deferred revenue fell to USD 449 million from USD 492 million, a small drag. EBITDA therefore turns into debt-service cash thinly and unevenly.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12; calculation D7; calculation D8; calculation D10
### Competitive forces

Rivalry is intense: the company describes new casinos, tribal expansion and large Las Vegas developments, and it took 2025 impairments in three Regional reporting units because localized competition lowered expected cash flows, so rivalry already reduces asset values. New entrants face licensing barriers, but new online jurisdictions and tribal supply still add competition. Substitutes are growing: prediction markets, sweepstakes products, daily fantasy sports and lotteries compete for the same spend. Buyer power is high because customers can switch properties and apps, and promotional spending in digital was USD 249 million in nine months. Supplier power sits with unions, performers and the landlords who set rent; the landlords are the most material for creditors.
### Macro, regulatory and technology factors

Regulation and taxes are material to credit because gaming taxes take 15.73% of revenue and are raised on digital wagers in some states, and because the merger needs gaming approvals. Economic conditions matter through discretionary spending, floating-rate borrowing of USD 5,800 million and rent escalators tied to consumer prices. Technology matters through the digital platform and the 2023 data incident, which led to class actions with losses reasonably possible but not estimable. These factors change leverage, free cash flow and refinancing capacity, so they are primary drivers rather than background.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 43; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 54; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 120–121; calculation D13; calculation D18
### SWOT in credit terms

Strengths: liquidity of USD 2,947 million with USD 142 million due before 2028, falling debt and debt interest, four diversified segments, and flexibility in growth capital expenditure. Weaknesses: lease-style obligations outside debt, falling Las Vegas earnings, 47.48% of principal due in 2029 and 2030, and thin goodwill cushions. Opportunities that could improve credit: iGaming growth in new states, payback from recent Regional capital expenditure at Lake Tahoe and New Orleans, and a merger that leaves debt in place or repays it from equity. Threats that could weaken credit: a leveraged buyout structure, persistent Las Vegas softness, higher gaming taxes and substitution by prediction markets.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 98; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 46; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 56–57; calculation D14
### Financial profile and credit quality

The financial profile rests on adequate liquidity and falling debt, and is constrained by fixed charges and a weak cash conversion. Debt is 3.60x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA and net debt 3.33x, but with lease-style obligations leverage is 7.70x, and secured principal is 2.90x EBITDA ahead of senior unsecured notes of USD 2,300 million. The trend is flat to slightly worse: issuer-adjusted EBITDA fell from USD 3,739 million in FY2024 to USD 3,573 million, net losses attributable to Caesars were USD 533 million over the last twelve months, and free cash flow improved only through lower capital expenditure. Missing datapoints are covenant headroom, the executed lease and debt documents, and how the merger is financed.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 15–16; calculation D5; calculation D16; calculation D19
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the credit depends on Las Vegas stabilising, the merger path and the 2028 maturities. Management expects strong free cash flow in 2026 on operating momentum, lower cash interest and lower capital expenditure, and the 2026 results to date are consistent with that, but Las Vegas, Regional margins and the lease escalator in November 2026 are headwinds. The merger's outside date can extend to November 27, 2027, and the revolver and Term Loan A mature on January 31, 2028, so refinancing must be addressed inside that window. Over three to five years the rent schedule rises to USD 1,468 million in 2030 while USD 5,536 million of debt matures in 2029 and 2030; digital legalization and capital expenditure payback are tailwinds, and gaming taxes, labor and competition are headwinds.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-04-28_ex991-2026q1ceiearningsrel.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; 10-K_2025-12-31_czr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 117; calculation D12; calculation D14
### Downside scenario

The downside starts with Las Vegas visitation and convention demand staying weak while Regional margins keep compressing under labor and gaming-tax costs. The first break is Adjusted EBITDA falling faster than revenue, as Las Vegas already did, and rent and debt interest do not fall with it. A 16.29% fall in issuer-adjusted EBITDA would erase free cash flow and would take lease-adjusted debt to 8.27x from 6.93x, and cutting growth and digital capital expenditure would extend that point to a 24.97% to 25.66% fall. Liquidity of USD 2,947 million and no material maturity before 2028 mean resilience looks sufficient to avoid distress for roughly a year, but the revolver and Term Loan A would then need extending from weaker earnings. The scenario is an illustration at the break-even point, not a forecast, and the observable triggers are Las Vegas Adjusted EBITDA, Regional margin, revolver drawings and any extension of the 2028 facilities.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_czr-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation D9; calculation D10; calculation D11; calculation D20
### Overall credit view

Overall, Caesars presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, segment diversification, a loyalty program and an owned digital platform, but credit quality is constrained by USD 13,188 million of lease-style obligations outside debt, falling Las Vegas earnings and thin cash conversion. Cash-flow durability appears adequate for the next year and weak against a sustained earnings decline. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on extending the revolver and Term Loan A before January 2028, on the treatment of existing debt in the merger and on stable earnings into the 2029 and 2030 maturities. The primary downside path is Las Vegas and Regional earnings declining against fixed and escalating rent. Further analysis would require the merger financing terms, the executed debt and lease documents, covenant definitions and peer data. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: earnings decline against fixed lease-style obligations.

## Gaps

- The merger financing, the buyer's ownership and the treatment of existing notes, loans and leases are not described in any supplied document, so the refinancing and leverage conclusions assume existing debt stays in place; this is a material gap closed by the merger agreement and the merger proxy statement.

- Covenant definitions and compliance certificates are not supplied, so headroom on the leverage and fixed charge covenants and the lease coverage test cannot be calculated; this is a material gap closed by the credit agreement, the indentures and the lease agreements.

- No ratings, market prices, peer financials or management projections are supplied, so the profile against typical leveraged-credit issuers and any forecast are not established; this is a minor gap for the selected pathway.

- Segment trends include Caesars Windsor from March 3, 2026 and Grand Bazaar from May 1, 2026 without a stated contribution, and discrete quarterly cash flows are not printed; these are minor gaps that make last-twelve-months and trend figures constructions.

- The outcome of the Atlantic City and Las Vegas dealer labor agreements that reached their expiration dates in 2026 and the range of loss from the Data Incident claims are not stated; these are minor gaps in the labor and legal risk read.
